newsitem.title: UK: UK government digs in heels on food safety record.
newsitem.headline: UK government digs in heels on food safety record.

text.p: Beleaguered Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg accused the opposition Labour party on Wednesday of scare-mongering over food safety as he unveiled an eight-point plan to raise hygiene standards in Britain's slaughterhouses.
Hogg spelled out the measures in a statement to parliament aimed at giving the government breathing room after a week of Labour-orchestrated attacks over its food safety record.

In a robust defence of his much-criticised ministry, Hogg said reports on meat safety circulated by Labour had been misleading because they did not take account of important progress made over the last 18 months.

"I do not pretend that there is not scope for further improvement. But I can assure the House (of Commons) that the Ministry of Agriculture... and the Meat Hygiene Service had been and remained determined to drive up standards and we are succeeding," he said.
Food safety has become headline news in Britain because of the crisis over mad cow disease and a recent food poisoning outbreak in Scotland that killed 20 people.

Labour has added to the government's discomfit over the past week by leaking and highlighting various reports by veterinary experts and meat inspectors accusing ministers of turning a blind eye to problems of poor hygiene in abattoirs.
But Hogg said the government had acted firmly to raise slaughterhouse standards and was drawing up an eight-point action plan to drive them even higher.

"Every plant now knows where its weak points are. Plants which are found repeatedly to have low standards will face progressively stricter attention from the meat inspectors and, as I have said, in appropriate cases prosecutions will ensue.
"Our purpose is to bring our abattoir practice up to the highest possible standards," Hogg said.
Labour's agriculture spokesman, Gavin Strang, repeated his party's demands for an independent food standards agency to restore public confidence.
Attacking Hogg, Strang said: "He is not effectively tackling these problems. There is no confidence in him, nor his government, as far as food safety issues are concerned."
But Hogg, whose job might have been on the line if an election were not just weeks away, turned the tables on Labour.
He accused it of "irresponsible scare-mongering" that would damage not only Britain's meat industry but also the country's standing in Europe.
"The fact that it's hysterical, irresponsible and ill-informed will not be understood in Europe. They will simply treat it at face value," Hogg said.

The row is unlikely to go away. Labour, favourite to win an election widely expected on May 1, believes food safety is a vote winner and says the government's record on the issue is an example of what it sees as ministerial drift and incompetence.
Hogg admitted that Labour would probably produce more documents in coming days aimed at embarrassing the government.
